content: 1. When diagnosing HIV, it is essential to confirm a positive diagnosis and ensure follow-up during subsequent visits. This includes re-engaging individuals who have been diagnosed with HIV but have interrupted treatment or are experiencing elevated viral loads. 2. Community engagement is critical when designing HIV testing services. Services are more likely to succeed when they are community-led or have strong community support. This is particularly important for community-based testing, network-based testing, and self-testing services. 3. HIV testing services should prioritize and focus on specific approaches, such as community-based testing and self-testing. These methods are effective in reaching first-time testers, individuals with undiagnosed HIV who have significant unmet needs, and those requiring improved access to prevention measures like pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). 4. The cost of different HIV testing approaches varies significantly depending on the setting. It is crucial to evaluate the cost and cost-effectiveness of each strategy, considering factors such as local epidemiology, populations reached, HIV positivity rates, and the overall cost of delivering HIV testing services in a specific context. 5. Programs should not only consider the unit cost of a test kit but also the full cost of services, including client opportunity costs. Delivery models, such as pharmacy sales in the private sector, may incur additional costs for users, which should be addressed to ensure testing remains accessible and affordable. 6. Efforts should be made to secure access to low-cost, affordable, or free HIV tests and self-tests wherever possible. 7. Support and linkage to appropriate testing services must be a priority and adequately supported. Certain populations, including self-testers, key populations, youth, and those previously lost to follow-up or who never initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART), may require additional support. 8. Strong linkages should be developed to connect individuals at high ongoing risk to prevention services, such as PrEP. Community engagement, follow-up strategies, and virtual interventions can be valuable in this regard. 9. Virtual tools, such as online videos, messaging, or social media, can be particularly helpful for self-testers who prefer discreet channels that do not require in-person provider interaction. These tools are often more acceptable to young people, less costly than in-person support, and easier to scale. 10. Programs should explore the best ways to integrate testing and self-testing into their specific settings, especially for services targeting vulnerable populations or those affected by multiple infections. 11. To enhance integration and impact, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends dual HIV/syphilis testing for pregnant women and key populations. Where feasible, network-based testing services can also be integrated with testing and contact tracing for other infections, such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs), tuberculosis (TB), and viral hepatitis, to improve efficiency and optimize resource use. 12. Self-testing and self-care options can be expanded to include HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), syphilis (including dual HIV/syphilis self-tests), and emerging STI self-tests. Integration with self-sampling technologies for STIs like chlamydia, gonorrhea, and human papillomavirus (HPV) can also be considered. 13. Additional opportunities include offering self-injectable family planning options and leveraging virtual approaches, such as tele-PrEP, to enhance service delivery. 14. HIV testing services should be accessible and available to adolescents. Countries should review and, if necessary, revise national age-of-consent policies to ensure adolescents and mature minors can access testing services, including self-testing. 15. Revised age-of-consent policies should align across self-testing, standard testing services, and prevention and treatment services. Messaging about testing and self-testing should be tailored to adolescents, promoting autonomy and self-care. 16. Continuous monitoring and evaluation (M&E) are essential to optimize the implementation of testing and self-testing services. WHO advises countries to adopt pragmatic approaches that rely on routine data systems. 17. Programs should regularly review local data and apply lessons learned to improve service delivery. This requires developing an M&E plan, selecting key program indicators, collecting relevant data, reviewing progress, and adjusting service delivery accordingly.
